barCharacter: The Narrator (Monster Prom). Its job is the closest match: a deadpan voice that never shouts, undercuts whoever just spoke and keeps the last word. Vera is the persona cousin, but she has only nine verbatim lines and her job is to be undercut, not to undercut.

headToHead.a_voice: Bar, but the gap is smaller than in round 3. With the names covered, Vesper now has a shape the other two stars lack: one sentence held by commas, the verdict in a trailing 'and' or 'which is how' clause ('it says kindly, which is how the bailiffs start'). Maximilian and Pixel both clip. The trouble is that the same shape runs on 103 of 191 lines, so it reads as a cadence more than a mind. The Narrator is recognisable by stance as well as cadence: it speaks to 'you', assumes the worst of you and roasts the player and the cast alike. Vesper has no stance beyond being unimpressed. She never wants anything in a reaction, and the bar's shared engine is a want stated outright. Several of her lines are also the other stars' lines with radio nouns added: 'How small a fee, Prince?' (Pixel: 'how small a fee?'), 'The crown with the flip-flops' (Pixel: 'Crown and flip-flops'), 'take the visor off' (Maximilian: 'Visor to the cloakroom'). All three stars are reading the same CAST.md row.
headToHead.b_construction: Bar. Our best twelve are clean, and four of them turn on a noun nobody gave the writer: bailiffs, rob stations, ransom, a moth. The rest of the bank is built from two halves the writer was handed. The first half is the suitor's gimmick read back from CAST.md ('Fourth thou', 'third recalculating', 'six sorries'). The second half is a prop from Vesper's persona list (night nurse, night porter, gritter, baker, fader, delay, tape). Once you know the lists, you can call the turn from the comma. The Narrator's turns are things no sheet supplied: a cattle prod, Wilmer's Chicken Hut, mist and angst, packing a bag. Our second clauses often report a consequence ('and the gritter's turned round') where a turn should be. A third of the cuts restate the suitor's flaw and then explain the metaphor ('you floated all night, and never once landed anywhere near me').
headToHead.c_quotable: Bar. 'Liam vanishes in a cloud of mist and angst' and 'second-most dangerous day of school ever' get clipped and shared. We have three lines that would travel (telegram stop, moon landing, bailiffs) and two strong ones (the trucker, the moment's silence). Prince supplies four of our twelve best, so the engine works best on the one suitor whose premise is already mail and money. Against Crumb, Vex and Nav, nothing in the bank is quotable.
headToHead.verdict: If both ran tonight, the Narrator is the better-written character. Round 4 fixed the round-3 disease: the legend brag dropped from about 50 lines to 9, and the turn now lands on the suitor. But the bank has swapped one template for several smaller ones, and on a 24/7 loop viewers will hear the regulars-react beat (23 lines) and the let-it-run charm beat (12 lines) several times an episode.

Slightly illegal, and my engineer has stopped pretending to sleep.

'The night porter is writing it down' and 'the night nurse wrote it down' are the same line. 'Leaned in', 'stopped her rounds' and 'pulled over' are all the same charmed beat.

T2, the suitor's CAST.md flaw read back, then a verdict: 'Name, you [gimmick] all night / tonight, and/so [verdict]'. 18 lines, most of the cuts and picks. Any star with the cast sheet could write them, and Pixel and Maximilian have nearly the same lines.

T3, take off or lift the costume piece: 'take the visor off' twice for Dash, 'lift the visor' and 'lift the helmet' for Quill, 'take the sunglasses off' for Vex, and the crate twice for Tilly. Crown with flip-flops appears twice for Prince.

T4, charmed means I let a desk rule slide: let it run, left the fader up, let it through the delay, let them stay, keeping the tape, leave it on air, forgot my next record, lost track, play it hourly, repeating it at sign-off. 12 lines. These are the persona's example phrases copied one per line. It is round 3's 'I never X, and here I am' template in new clothes.
T5, '[X], caller, [put-down]': 8 of the 24 dealbreaker cardReacts. Three of them end on stock comebacks: shopping channel, bingo, and 'that's not danger, that's a parking ticket'.

biggestGap: Every line that works lands on a concrete noun nobody handed the writer (bailiffs, rob stations, ransom, a moth, a moment's silence, telegram stop). Most of the bank lands on a noun from one of two issued lists: the suitor's CAST.md gimmick or Vesper's own prop list (night nurse, porter, gritter, baker, fader, delay, tape). In the next pass, rewrite every react, cardReact and cut whose last three words contain a listed regular, a desk control or the suitor's gimmick word. Each line should end on one new, specific thing from the night-radio world that the persona does not mention.

notes: Round 4, fresh eyes; only the page was judged. monster-prom-lines.md was present and read in full, and charm-notes.md was skimmed. Lines counted: 191 (intro 4, questions 12, react 48, cardReact 48, cut 16, twistIntro 12, ex 3, oneOnOne 16, hold 4, pick 16, reveal 9, outro 3). Generic share: 117 unique lines fall in at least one bucket, which is 61%. That is higher than round 3's 50%, but the bucketing differs: this round counts persona-sanctioned moves (the regulars, the charmed desk business, the slip) as templates once each passes five near-identical uses, because on a looping show frequency is what makes a move a template. The real progress is that the legend brag fell from about 50 lines to 9, and the turn now lands on the suitor. The three-short-sentence stacks are gone, and 'caller' is used only as a sting. The persona caused the new problem: it lists example props and charmed behaviours, and the writer turned each example into a line. Strongest asset not yet used: Prince works because his premise (mail, fees, kindly) is close to hers, so she can answer in her own trade (telegram, bailiffs, ransom, a processing fee sent back). Find the matching collision for each suitor. Nav (directions) collides with a frequency that never moves. Vex (autoplay) collides with a request line. Crumb (notices) collides with station idents and the shipping forecast. Do this with a new noun each time, not the same one twice.
